title: Analysis | Why Kerala's Congress govt wants to keep VIPs' corruption cases top secret & quell RTI pleas
content: When the Oommen Chandy-led UDF government issued an order exempting the T (Top Secret) branch of the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) from the Right to Information (RTI) purview in 2016, it was alleged that it was part of a move to stem the flow of information on vigilance probes against ministers and officials ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections. The bar bribery scam and the solar case had hovered over the UDF government then. While the VACB gave a clean chit to the then Finance Minister K M Mani in the bar bribery case, the government still had reasons to shield sensitive information with the VACB, especially as the front geared up for the elections. Strange timing This is why the timing of the latest order from the UDF government, taking two top secret sections of the VACB out of the RTI ambit, piques interest. The Vigilance had already cleared Chief Minister V D Satheesan of corruption in the Punarjani housing scheme, which the CPM had vehemently used to hound him. Satheesan, for all his easy, charming eloquence on transparency, has been adamant about not uttering a word on his controversial chopper ride. Even questions on the helicopter ride in the ongoing Assembly session remain unanswered. If at all a corruption complaint is filed with the VACB on the chopper issue, the High Court has already ordered that no information on an ongoing inquiry shall be furnished by the VACB. The UDF went ahead with the order while the Congress has been riven by a rift over the government's purported soft stand towards former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan in the CMRL-Exalogic case. When the dissent over the decision to go for a preliminary inquiry became uproarious, the KPCC chief was even forced to issue a gag order on public statements. The HC is set to consider Pinarayi's appeal against the vigilance FIRs in the CMRL bribery case on Monday. With the latest order in effect, if the file is moved to the T sections, no query can be filed under the RTI. However, even without this order, no information could be accessed otherwise for a probe in progress. The order to exempt the T1 and T2 sections of the VACB from the provisions of the RTI Act was issued by the General Administration Department on October 22. The T1 section deals with high-level, sensitive vigilance investigations, secret inquiries and maintenance of high-security files, while the T2 section pertains to source reports, coordination of surprise inspections, and collection and analysis of intelligence-related information. The government had earlier exempted eight institutions/organisations of the State Intelligence and Security Organisations from the purview in 2006: Special Branch CID, Crime Branch CID, District Special Branches, District and Crime Record Bureaux, Police Telecommunication Unit, Confidential Branch in Police HQ, State and Regional Forensic Labs, and State and District Finger Print Bureaux. Legal hurdles RTI specialists, former information commissioners and legal experts flag serious technical flaws in the government notification. The government showed unnecessary haste in issuing this order. The Assembly session is in progress, and yet it enforced the order through an extraordinary gazette. As per the rule, every notification under sub-section 4 shall be laid before the legislature. It has not been done in this case. The State Information Commissioner was not consulted. Generally, information on an investigation in progress need not be furnished via RTI; with this order, they have ensured that even after the completion of the inquiry, the report will not be made available in the public domain, said A A Hakkim, former State Information Commissioner. The fundamental legal question is whether Section 24(4) can be invoked to impose a blanket restriction on information that is otherwise not exempt from disclosure under Sections 8 and 9...
